'''Jeff William Lichtman''' (born 1951) is an American [[neuroscientist]].<ref name=nas14/> He is the [[Jeremy R. Knowles]] Professor of Molecular and Cellular Biology and [[Santiago Ramón y Cajal]] Professor of Arts and Sciences at [[Harvard University]]. He is best known for his pioneering work developing  the [[neuroimaging]] [[Connectomics|connectomic]] technique known as [[Brainbow]].<ref name="Brouillette">{{cite journal |last1=Brouillette |first1=Monique |title=Mapping the brain to understand the mind |journal=Knowable Magazine |date=21 April 2022 |doi=10.1146/knowable-042122-1 |url=https://knowablemagazine.org/article/mind/2022/mapping-brain-understand-mind|doi-access=free |language=en}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Lichtman was born in [[Salt Lake City]], [[Utah]] in 1951. He grew up in the [[Northeastern United States]].<ref name=nas14/> Lichtman received a BA from [[Bowdoin College]] in 1973. In 1980, he received both MD and PhD from [[Washington University in St. Louis]], where he was advised by [[Dale Purves]]. After completing postdoctoral work at [[Harvard Medical School]], he established his lab at [[Washington University School of Medicine]] and conducted research there for 30 years.<ref name=labbio>{{cite web|url=https://lichtmanlab.fas.harvard.edu/people/jeff-lichtman|title=Jeff W. Lichtman, MD, PhD|publisher=Harvard University|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref><ref name=nas14/>

In 2004, he was appointed [[Jeremy R. Knowles]] Professor of Molecular and Cellular Biology  at [[Harvard University]]. In 2013, he was named the inaugural [[Santiago Ramón y Cajal]] Professor, a five-year appointment intended to recognize outstanding research and teaching.<ref name=gazette2013>{{cite web|url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2013/03/first-santiago-ramon-y-cajal-professor-of-arts-and-sciences/|title=First Santiago Ramón y Cajal Professor is named|author=Reuell P|date=11 March 2013|publisher=Harvard Gazette|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref> Lichtman is a faculty member within the Harvard Center for Brain Science and the Conte Center at Harvard University.<ref name=conte>{{cite web|url=http://www.conte.harvard.edu/investigators/jeff-lichtman-md-phd/|title=Jeff Lichtman, MD, PhD|publisher=Conte Center|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref> From 2013 to 2016, he was a Grass Foundation Trustee.<ref name=grass13>{{cite web|url=https://www.grassfoundation.org/people/jeff-w-lichtman|title=Jeff W. Lichtman|publisher=Grass Foundation|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref>

==Research==
[[File:Brainbow_(Lichtman_2008).jpg|thumb|500px|alt=Three Brainbow images|Up to ~160 colours were observed in the first Brainbow mice. (a) A [[motor nerve]] innervating ear muscle. (b) An axon tract in the [[brainstem]]. c) The [[dentate gyrus]]. From Lichtman and Sanes, 2008.<ref name=brainbow>{{cite journal|author=Lichtman JW, Livet J, Sanes JR|title=A technicolour approach to the connectome.|journal=Nat Rev Neurosci|year=2008|volume=9|issue=6|pages=417–22|pmid=18446160|doi=10.1038/nrn2391|pmc=2577038}}</ref>]]
The Lichtman lab studies [[activity-dependent plasticity]] in [[motor system|motor]] and [[autonomic nervous system|autonomic]] circuits of living animals. Lichtman hypothesizes that [[axon]]s undergo [[synaptic pruning]] and strengthening in response to experiences, and these experiences cause neurons which co-innervate the same cell to compete for dominance, thereby driving [[synaptic plasticity]]. The lab uses [[genetically modified mouse|genetically modified mice]] and automated imaging tools to identify [[neural circuit]] motifs throughout the nervous system.<ref name=labbio/>

In 2007, Lichtman and [[Joshua R. Sanes]] first published the [[Brainbow]] '''mouse''' method, in which different fluorescent proteins are expressed stochastically in neighboring neurons within a mouse's [[nervous system]], thereby allowing neighboring neuronal processes to be distinguishable by [[fluorescence microscopy]]. Subsequently, this technique has been adapted and used to map neural circuits in mice, ''[[Caenorhabditis elegans]]'', and ''[[Drosophila melanogaster]]''.<ref name=labbio/><ref name=spectrum15>{{cite web|url=https://www.spectrumnews.org/news/toolbox/rainbow-of-dyes-maps-neurons-tangled-paths-in-brain/|title=Rainbow of dyes maps neurons' tangled paths in brain|author=Yandell K|date=13 May 2015|website=Spectrum News|publisher=Simons Foundation|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref>

Additionally, the Lichtman lab developed a  device called the Automatic Tape-Collecting Lathe Ultramicrotome (ATLUM),<ref name=labbio/><ref name=cbsatlum>{{cite web|url=http://cbs.fas.harvard.edu/science/connectome-project/atlum|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100412115223/http://cbs.fas.harvard.edu/science/connectome-project/atlum|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 12, 2010|title=ATLUM|website=Center for Brain Science|publisher=Harvard University|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref> which can be used for automated [[electron microscopy]] in [[neural circuit reconstruction]]. Data from the Lichtman lab has been used in the [[citizen science]] game [[EyeWire]], developed in collaboration with [[Sebastian Seung]] and [[Winfried Denk]], to construct a full [[connectome]] of the mouse [[retina]].<ref name=nyt2014>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/05/27/science/all-circuits-are-busy.html|title=All Circuits Are Busy|author=Gorman J|date=26 May 2014|work=The New York Times|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref><ref name=guardian2012>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2012/may/07/quest-connectome-mapping-brain|title=Quest for the connectome: scientists investigate ways of mapping the brain|author=Sample I|date=7 May 2012|work=The Guardian|access-date=9 May 2019}}</ref>

The  lab is also interested in [[Inhibitory postsynaptic potential|inhibitory]] [[interneuron]]s in the [[prefrontal cortex]], which are thought to be selectively vulnerable in [[mental disorder]]s such as [[autism]] or [[schizophrenia]].<ref name=labbio/><ref name=conte/>
